input: This executive summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and considers whether the project is ready to move forward. The plant currently uses 1852 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which represents a very substantial part of its overall energy picture. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 16% of that electricity use, which works out at a derived saving of 296 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $374k, and at an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k, giving a derived simple payback of 12.5 years, which is a long time over which to recover an investment of this size. It is important to note that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, and it is also worth noting that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month has not been modelled, so there are open questions on both the size and the shape of the projected saving of 296 MWh per year. In light of all of this, the recommendation is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected saving can be tested against measured data; in other words, the plant would be committing $374k of capital in return for a derived annual saving of $30k, which is precisely why the payback stretches to 12.5 years and why the figures are being treated with some caution at this stage. The plant engineer owns the trial.
target: Recommendation: run a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 1852 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 296 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost is $374k. At an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 12.5 years. The payback states the weakness of the case as projected: 12.5 years is a long recovery for a figure that has not been measured. The saving is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the 296 MWh per year carries two open questions, its size at this plant and its shape across the year. A metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines answers the first question on measured data and bounds the second, because a line under meter shows both the saving it makes and the months in which it makes it. Until the trial reports, the decision the figures support is the trial itself, not the retrofit. The capital decision would commit $374k against a derived annual saving of $30k that rests on a projection; the trial converts the projection into a measurement on one line before the commitment is made, and the plant engineer's ownership of the trial puts the measurement in the hands of the engineer who will have to run the retrofit if it follows.
